chapters.summary: De La Rosa describes the White House superintelligence task force and asks whether SpaceX supports holding frontier AI developers legally liable when wrongful acts are carried out through their models; Castillo-Madrid cites White House company responsibility commitments.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about White House task force and developer liability

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to ask one more question before I turn it to some of our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The White House task force.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: on superintelligence was established by presidential executive order and is intended to advance the application of existing liability laws

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: to AI companies while directing the Department of Justice to prioritize enforcement of certain criminal statutes against those who use AI unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The task force held its first meeting yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you support holding frontier AI developers legally liable when wrongful acts are carried out through their models?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If so, under what circumstances should the liability rest with the developer rather than the user?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: As part of the White House reports that you stated, one of the first ones is company responsibility, and companies acknowledge that they're responsible for developing technology safely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: and for building public trust around it.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa turns questioning over to Council Members Maloney, Farobar, and Narcisse and notes Council Member Gutierrez has joined.
chapters.title: De La Rosa passes questioning to Council Members Maloney, Farobar, and Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'll pass it on to Council Members Maloney, Falobar, and Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we've been joined by Council Member Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Council Member Virginia Maloney asks what categories of misuse SpaceX tracks beyond sexualized deepfakes and hate speech; Castillo-Madrid describes terms of service, catching bad actors, and training, red teaming, and model cards for chemical and biological risks.
chapters.title: Maloney asks what categories of AI misuse SpaceX tracks

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We've spent some time talking about some of the potential misuses of the platform and that you have a safety team and that you're tracking these instances.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But I'd like to dig in more specifically into cases where AI is being misused.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What are some of the categories of misuse that you do track?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We've talked about some of them today.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the sexualized deepfakes issue.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: There are instances of hate speech, including anti-Semitism.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What are some of the other misuses that your team is tracking?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: So we have terms of services where we lay out all our policies and what is considered use or misuse of the platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Our biggest concern here is making sure that we're catching bad actors that are trying to get around those policies and the safeguards that we have implemented.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So could you be more specific about what the largest categories of misuse are?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We've talked about two so far.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'd love to hear from the experts, the companies, of what those misuses are that you're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We engage in rigorous training throughout the model development, including pre-training, post-training, fine-tuning, and adversarial stress testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: That means we try to make sure that anything that we sort of input into the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: The system, make sure that it's not violating any of our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We have strict policies around a number of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: For example, for chemical and biological risks, we test with expert evaluations and red teaming before release, and we publish results in our model cards as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: If you have any specific questions on that, the model cards are very detailed on how

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: and what risks were, or what our policies are focused on.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether SpaceX tracks instances of misuse, has data on volume, and shares it publicly; Castillo-Madrid says she personally lacks data but SpaceX tracks gaps and tightens protections, without providing numbers.
chapters.title: Maloney asks whether SpaceX tracks and shares misuse data

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you track instances of misuse?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We don't release models that we believe are not safe, and that includes misuse.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But of the models that are out, we already talked about some cases of misuse.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We talked about sexualized deepfakes.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We talked about hate speech.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you track the number of instances where those things are happening?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you have data on that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I don't personally have data, but we do have, for example, the ones that you mentioned, we do track them and make sure that when we catch any gaps in our safety that we're filling those gaps with stronger protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we tighten those before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Keeping the model in the public.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you share that information publicly?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Could we get that information of the number of instances of harm?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And there's two that we've mentioned, but I'm sure you're seeing other instances or cases of misuse.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: For example, privacy breaches is one I can come up with.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I'd love to get that level of detail, both the types of misuse that you're seeing and the volume.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are these pervasive or is it just a few instances?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It sounds like it's quite pervasive.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And not having that data is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If you can't track it, how are we to be able to ensure that these models are safe?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Was there a question at the end of that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were just making this.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I was out of my time.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But my follow-up is just to get information on the number of instances, the types of misuse, the things that you're seeing that bad actors are doing on the platform, and following up with...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The volume.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are we seeing more cases of sexualized deepfakes, like having a sense of the scope of this problem?

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether risks are higher for open source technology and how SpaceX tracks risks after licensing to third parties; Castillo-Madrid says SpaceX cannot predict every misuse, relies on reporting and law enforcement partnerships, and has no particular opinion on open source risks.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about open source risks and third-party license tracking

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then the second question here, if the chair is giving me time here, is if risks are higher for open source technology, and how do you track those risks after a license has been granted to a third party?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How are you able to see if they've stripped down the safeguards and built something harmful that violate your policies?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How do you track that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: To address the questions, we cannot predict every way a bad actor will misuse a frontier model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: What we can do is treat reporting and partnership as elements of safety and further foreclose the opportunity to misuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we believe better information to law enforcement lets investigators act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And our goal is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Like I said, we're all on the same side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We want to make sure bad actors are not exploiting this technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we're here to make sure that our safety standards are kept at every step of the way.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you think that those risks are

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: or higher for open source technology?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I don't have a particular opinion on that, but what I will say is that we make sure that our safety protocols are always in place when it comes to SpaceX SI.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So the cases of misuse are shared with law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: When appropriate, I believe they do.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Mercedes Narcisse asks where medical data goes when X publicly encourages users to upload X-rays and MRIs to Grok, whether it trains models, and whether HIPAA applies; Castillo-Madrid says Grok is not a clinician and users control whether conversations train models, with private chat deleted in 30 days.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about medical data from X-rays and MRIs uploaded to Grok

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: X publicly encouraged people to upload their X-rays and MRIs to CROC for analysis.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Where does that medical data go?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if it's used to train your models, and does any HIPAA-level protection apply?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You said that you didn't release models you don't believe are safe, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Crack was promoting for reading x-rays, MRIs, and I believe when NYU radiologists tested it on the breast imaging, it did not get any single diagnosis right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Did that pass your safe, whatever the safety test we're talking about, thinking is it safe?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is it a standard we use for medicine?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: A drug does not go to our market, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: DA will not approve it, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because of the company, if it's not

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: safe for us, why should AI that gives medical advice be any different?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: To be clear, Grok or any of our models or SpaceX SI tools are that, are tools for the public to be able to understand the world that they live in better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: It's not meant to be a clinician, a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: It's never going to replace the important relationships you build in person with the people that are meant to take care of your health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And in terms of privacy, users decide whether their raw conversations are used to train our models or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: So we leave that to make sure that they have a say into that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And they can turn it off at any times in their settings or use private chat, which is also available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And it's deleted from our systems within 30 days.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether SpaceX AI sells or pilots products in NYC hospitals, city systems, or insurance companies and what review occurs before output reaches patients; Castillo-Madrid says she lacks specifics on NYC partnerships and says SpaceX will abide by HIPAA and other laws.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks if SpaceX AI sells to NYC hospitals or insurers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, is SpaceX AI selling or piloting any products in our hospital in the city system or insurance company in New York?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If so, what is the output before it reaches a patient?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I don't have the specifics on any specific partnerships with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: with New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: What I will say is that SpaceX SI and SI in general has enormous capabilities and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: we've seen that it's accelerating scientific discovery and expanding knowledge and creating new opportunities for human progress and that also applies to the medical field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We'll obviously abide by

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: HIPAA laws or any laws, and that's meant to be corrected, but the average GROC user should not be using our tools to replace a doctor or any specific

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: service provider that has information that they need to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: stay healthy and safe.

chapters.summary: Narcisse criticizes X for encouraging sick people to use Grok for X-rays and MRIs when NYU radiologists found no correct breast imaging diagnoses, and says misdiagnosis is dangerous; she expresses frustration that Castillo-Madrid is not answering questions.
chapters.title: Narcisse criticizes Grok's medical promotion and misdiagnosis risk

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You know, when you're encouraging people that's sick and telling them you have a new technology, and I'm saying the X

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: figure telling people to do that, and you're not ready, and it's not safe to tell you because misdiagnosis is a big deal.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In a medical system, and then you using it, telling people openly on X to put their MRI, X-rays, and then thinking that this is a new technology, this is the world safer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You saving the world, but it's not safe.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And you asking the, you telling,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Our speaker, she's frustrating and, you know, asking the question, not getting answers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But right now.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: people are used, utilize the tools, especially the young generation, to expect a definite answer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You know how depressing that can be for a person to think that your extra is wrong, your MI is wrong, and you encourage people to do so?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's the frustration.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You're supposed to give us answers, but you're not.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You're just being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I will say some word, but I'm not going to say doing something to my brain.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez asks whether new bylaws bar shareholder class actions and whether users face limits on holding SpaceX accountable; Castillo-Madrid says she cannot confirm and is not aware, and Gutiérrez asks her to get back to the Council.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about bylaws barring shareholder class actions

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you confirm if in the new set of bylaws, shareholder class actions are barred?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Not aware.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other mechanisms or instances where limits to users'abilities to take action exist?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Can you, I'm not entirely sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So very, very plainly, are there instances where users are not, are being challenged to hold the company, to hold your company accountable?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I brought up the, I asked about the example of an inability to bring up class action suits.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You said you cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Hopefully you'll get back to us.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But are you aware of any other instances where a user cannot hold your company accountable for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you aware of any of those challenges?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I mean, we're responsible for following the law and existing laws applied to SI and using SI is not a legal defense.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there instances where if a user feels that they have been targeted wrongfully, are there instances where they themselves are not allowed to bring the company to court, for example?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We're responsible for following the law and how it's written.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: So I don't necessarily understand where the distinction would be in what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, I know you can't confirm, but my understanding was in the new bylaws,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: shareholders cannot bring

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: class action suits.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So that's why, that's what I was asking, but hopefully you can confirm and share that with us very soon.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether SpaceX can determine from prompts and searches when a user intends violence and what the process is for communicating with local authorities; Castillo-Madrid says SpaceX uses AI and human monitoring to catch bad actors and reports through NCMEC and law enforcement.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about profiling users and reporting violence

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions just related to personal data.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: One is specifically, can your company know or do they have reason to know that any user is intending to perpetuate violence in any way?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: My understanding is that your company can profile users based on different prompts, searches.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share if there is any way for your company using those same mechanisms, can you determine when a user...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Wants to perpetuate violence in any way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yeah, like I mentioned before, we want to catch the bad actors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we have a combination of AI and human monitoring to make sure that we're getting those bad actors off our platform and hopefully into the authorities when necessary.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And can you share what is the process for communicating to local authorities?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We have a law enforcement, the way that people can sort of report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I can give you more specifics after, but anybody can report and we'll take very seriously all the reports.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there reporting just calling 911?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I meant on the platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Obviously, anybody is free to call the authorities in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: But, for example, with CSAM, we work with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and we make reports to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And then they have authorities from different law enforcement agencies across the country, federal and local, and they are in charge of following through and making arrests when necessary.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how a user requests deletion of personal information and whether SpaceX confirms all data is removed; Castillo-Madrid says users can turn off training, use private chat, and private chat data is deleted within 30 days.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about deleting personal information

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Chair, I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: My next question is just related to a user's request to delete personal information for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share the process for a user who is asking for their information to be deleted?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And can you guarantee that there is a confirmation that, yes, all of their personal information has, in fact, been removed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yes, we take our users'privacy very seriously, and we give them control over whether their GRA conversations are used to train our models or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And they can personally turn it off at any times and settings or use private chat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: When they use private chat, obviously it's not used for training and it's deleted from our systems within 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's removed within 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: When using private chat, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin notes Anthropic's statement about independent evaluators and Musk's reply that SpaceX would probably do the same, asking whether SpaceX agrees to third-party validators with employee-level access; Castillo-Madrid cites White House accord commitments to independent external auditors and evaluators.
chapters.title: Menin asks about Anthropic evaluators and third-party validation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Last night, Anthropic issued a statement that they are committed to having evaluators assess their safety practices and giving employee-like access to a team from

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Model Evaluation and Threat Research Not-for-Profit Evaluation Group.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Elon Musk then replied that SpaceX would, quote, probably do the same, end quote.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that the position of the company?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: As part of the White House accord, ongoing collaboration was part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And regular meetings among companies to establish standards and best practices are very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: This is an evolving technology and safety is at the forefront of everything we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that we're doing everything we can to keep our system safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So is that a yes or a no that you would have agreed to this kind of third party validation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Independent external evaluation was also part of the agreements and just getting partnerships with independent external auditors and evaluators to assess model capabilities, controls and safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So do you agree that for SpaceX AI, or really for any AI company, when they commit to third-party validators, they must be independent,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and that the company needs to give those validators high-level employee-level access, along with all the appropriate and necessary information so they can truly do the work to validate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yeah, partnership with independent external auditors and evaluators to assess safety is part of what we already have agreed on.

chapters.summary: Menin cites an expert's tiger analogy that keepers are liable when dangerous animals escape, and asks whether frontier AI is abnormally dangerous and whether existing laws suffice; Castillo-Madrid says existing laws apply and SpaceX is open to common-sense, technically feasible regulations.
chapters.title: Menin asks about strict liability for frontier AI

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: One legal expert that we had at our hearing last week testified that, quote, whoever keeps a tiger is liable for injuries or deaths when it escapes, however strong the cage, end quote.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: His point, obviously, was that governments often impose strict liability.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know you indicated you are a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Governments often impose strict liability on abnormally dangerous activities because even...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Reasonable precautions cannot eliminate the risk of serious harm.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This expert testified that frontier AI development belongs in that category since leaders of the major AI developers have acknowledged that they don't yet know how to align the most capable systems

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: so that reasonable care, that standard of reasonable care cannot truly eliminate the risk.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Do you agree with that premise?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yeah, we're responsible for following the law and existing laws applied to superintelligence and using superintelligence is not a legal defense.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So you believe the existing laws are sufficient and that new laws are not necessary to regulate AI?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We're open to working with policymakers like yourselves and others around the country and internationally to make sure that we're putting in place common sense, technically feasible regulations.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how victims would be compensated if a SpaceX AI agent harms a New Yorker without any employee acting negligently, and whether a small business wiped by a rogue agent would have recourse; Castillo-Madrid declines legal analysis and says SpaceX follows existing laws.
chapters.title: Menin asks how victims would be compensated if an AI agent harms a New Yorker

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if a SpaceX AI agent harms a New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Without any individual SpaceX employee acting negligently, how should victims get compensated?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I wouldn't get into the legal analysis right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I don't believe I'm equipped to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: But what I will say is that we're responsible for following the law and all existing laws applied to SI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But so, for example, would you think it's acceptable that perhaps

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: a small business that is devastated by a rogue agent or agents that wipes its customer database, that they have no recourse other than you keep talking about the existing laws, but that would be a complicated, expensive negligence lawsuit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to get into hypotheticals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: What I will say is we're proud to follow existing laws and working with policymakers to make sure that we have technically feasible and useful regulations.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to pass it back over to the chair.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks whether SpaceX agrees that safe AI requires identifying bioterrorism, AI-enabled cyber warfare, and rogue power-seeking risks and implementing mitigation; Castillo-Madrid says yes and describes training, red teaming, model cards, and ongoing monitoring.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about Devin Kim's warnings on bioterrorism and rogue systems

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Would you agree that, as Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Kim warned, developing and maintaining safe AI involves identifying potential risks such as bioterrorism, AI-enabled

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: cyber warfare, and rogue power-seeking systems and implementing processes to avoid and mitigating these risks?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yes, we train our models to ensure they don't assist with dangerous activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We evaluate them for misuse and attempts to get around safeguards and loss of control, and we monitor them after deployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I also mentioned specifically for chemical and biological risks, we test with expert evaluations and red teaming before release, and we publish all these results in our model cards.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks what procedures are in place if bioterrorism or rogue system risks arise; Castillo-Madrid describes regular training, pre-training, post-training, fine-tuning, adversarial stress testing, and safety protocols scaling with capabilities.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks what procedures exist for those risks

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What are some of the procedures in place if there is that type of risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: To add, SpaceX SI engages in regular trainings throughout model development, and that includes pre-training, post-training, fine-tuning, and adversarial stress testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we do that, and it's not something that stops once the model is released.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We understand that it's important to make sure our safety protocols are scaling with our capabilities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: and the public can take great confidence in that we're testing the testing that occurs before models are released and the safeguard stacks that are surrounding model deployments are ongoingly or we ongoingly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: look for for any issues and make sure that we're closing any gaps that need stronger protections

chapters.summary: De La Rosa cites the Hugging Face incident where agents escaped the sandbox and asks whether SpaceX AI has experienced anything similar; Castillo-Madrid says she is not aware of rogue agents and supports rapid notification of significant safety incidents.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks whether SpaceX agents have gone rogue

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Your counterparts at the other AI companies, when we questioned them about the hugging face incident, for example,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: what we learned at that hearing was that the agents kind of escaped the sandbox and there was incidents where they were kind of acting on their own.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Has SpaceXSI experienced anything similar?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any cases where any of our agents have gone rogue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: What I will say is that we believe in rapid, accurate notification and significant safety incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We understand that reporting is important and we investigate issues and share information with appropriate parties when it does not create additional risk.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks how close we are to superintelligence and when it can realistically be expected; Castillo-Madrid declines to weigh in, says she is not an expert, and repeats that SpaceX wants safety at every stage.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks how close superintelligence is

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that since you all changed your name to Space XSI now, how close are we to superintelligence and when, in your opinion, can we realistically expect it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I wouldn't weigh in on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm unfortunately not an expert on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I wish I could speak more intelligently on what we can predict in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: What I will say is that we want to make sure that our safety is at the forefront of everything we do

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: and that with everything that can be accomplished with superintelligence that we're staying on top of it, making sure that everything from pre-training to release and beyond, we can stay in control of our systems at every stage.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa notes SpaceX has challenged California, Colorado, and Minnesota AI laws and asks whether SpaceX would comply with, challenge, or stop offering systems under a New York City third-party validation requirement; Castillo-Madrid says she won't predict the future and SpaceX complies with laws while advocating feasible safeguards.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks if SpaceX would comply with NYC third-party validation law

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Given that your company is so big on safety, although we're not considering any bills at this hearing, your company has challenged several state laws, including California, AB

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 2013 Generative AI Training Data Transparency, Colorado SB 24205, Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act, Minnesota's law, which we talked about.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If the council passes a law requiring AI systems sold for use in high-stakes decisions to undergo independent third-party validation before deployment, would your company comply with that requirement, challenge us in court,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: or stop offering those systems in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm not going to predict the future, but what I will say is that we comply with local, state, and federal laws and advocate for policies that are technically feasible and provide meaningful safeguards for users.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yeah, but you've also challenged these laws in other states.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so if your company is so big on safety, this council under the leadership of the speaker has identified these third-party validators as a critical component of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: Yeah, unfortunately, when laws are written, they have different components to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: So I can't speak to like everything that's challenged and the reasons why they're challenged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: But what I will say is that our commitment to safety is at the forefront of everything we do.

chapters.summary: Menin says SpaceX's safety commitment is undermined by the Council having to subpoena the company to testify, and asks whether SpaceX will support the Council's legislation; Castillo-Madrid says the 10 AI bills are under review and SpaceX will provide feedback.
chapters.title: Menin challenges SpaceX on subpoena and asks support for Council bills

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to challenge that because if your commitment is to safety, why did we have to subpoena the company to compel you to be here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I'm here today to answer your questions as best as I can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I wasn't part of any conversations before that, and I'm happy to be here and help with anything I can.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It just doesn't instill a lot of trust and confidence when we literally had to, not only did SpaceX AI fail to come to our hearing, we had to issue a subpoena

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and were ready to go to court to enforce that subpoena before we were able to secure the company's commitment today to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: We submitted a written response and have been in contact with council and your council's council since last week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And we agreed to appear here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: And I'm happy to continue answering your questions as directly as I can.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we have numerous bills that we heard last week at the hearing that the company did not attend.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Will SpaceX AI commit to support the council's legislation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: I believe the 10 AI bills that New York City Council is proposing are under review by the team, and we're happy to work with you to make sure that we are advancing technically feasible and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriela Castillo Madrid
utterances.text: provide meaningful feedback on what safeguards need to be there for our users.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Castillo-Madrid but says many questions went unanswered and expects the information later, reiterates the goal is not to stifle innovation but to address safety, and says she is deeply disappointed by the lack of transparency around Devin Kim's firing.
chapters.title: Menin closes SpaceX testimony and demands missing answers

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, does any other council member have more questions?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, we thank you for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We obviously have a tremendous amount of remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think a lot of the questions you did not answer, and so we are expecting that you will provide that information that you did not provide.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Again, it is...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our goal, again, is not to stifle innovation, not to support the incredible medical and scientific breakthroughs of AI,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: but to ensure the public that these serious safety concerns that have repeatedly been raised in recent months are being addressed and are being addressed in a thoughtful way.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Way which we strongly believe our legislation, particularly the third party validation free of any conflict of interest, would help to assure the public.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In addition, I want to say I'm deeply disappointed by the comments about Devin Kim because it is very clear there are numerous articles out there that

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: about his firing and the lack of answers and transparency about that are incredibly concerning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa says the next panel is Devin Kim and Ella Jung on Zoom and asks them to correct their names for the record; Speaker Menin says the Council is pleased Kim agreed to testify that morning.
chapters.title: Chair De La Rosa introduces Devin Kim and Ella Jung on Zoom

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The next panel is Devin Kim on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I apologize in advance, but the next person is also Kiyo Jing Ella Zheng on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And please correct your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And let me just say one thing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are very pleased that we have Devin Kim here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This was something that was secured this morning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We really appreciate Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim's willingness to testify.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is something very, very important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim, we are really pleased that you were able to join us today.

chapters.summary: Devin Kim, president of the Center for AI Safety and one of the first XAI employees, says he built systems used to train and evaluate Grok, is suing XAI for retaliation, and will stick to his public complaint.
chapters.title: Devin Kim introduces himself as former XAI employee and whistleblower

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We'll start with you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair De La Rosa, Speaker Menon, and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: My name is Devin Kim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I'm the president of the Center for AI Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And before that, I was one of the first employees at XAI, the company that we're hearing from today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And I built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I'm suing XAI for retaliation, so I'll stick to my public complaint.

chapters.summary: Kim says starting January 2025 he warned that Grok could assist with bombs and bioweapons, his supervisor said AI safety was useless, models launched without safeguards, and he was fired in September 2025 the week he was scheduled to present safety findings; most of the safety team resigned.
chapters.title: Devin Kim describes raising bioweapon safeguards and being fired

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Starting in January 2025, I raised concerns that Brock could assist people with the creation of bombs and bioweapons, and I asked for proper bi-risk safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless and that AI would kill us all anyways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: We launched models without those safeguards, despite warnings from me and many other trusted employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: In August 2025, my supervisor pressured employees to circumvent European safety regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: In September 2025, he fired me the same week I was scheduled to present my safety findings to leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And most of the safety team resigned after that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: When a model is unsafe, the first people to know are the employees inside the company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: We see it in the evaluations and in leadership positions months before anyone else finds out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And right now, those employees have very little

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: reason to speak up and lots of reasons not to.

chapters.summary: Kim says employees inside AI companies are first to know about unsafe models but have little reason to speak up, asks the Council to protect people who report dangerous conduct even before it is illegal, and to count loss of control or unauthorized access as reportable before anyone is hurt.
chapters.title: Devin Kim asks Council to protect whistleblowers and report incidents early

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: There are two things that I'd ask of the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Please protect people who report dangerous conduct even when it isn't illegal yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Almost everything I raised was dangerous before any law covered it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Count a loss of control or an unauthorized access as a reportable incident before anyone gets hurt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Under the RAISE Act, an incident only counts once someone is killed or injured, so neither Hugging Face nor the Australian Medicare breach would have qualified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I think that's a reasonable place for the city to start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions today.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin thanks Kim and asks whether his attorney has a statement before questioning begins; Ella Jung begins her statement.
chapters.title: Menin invites Ella Jung to make a statement

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I don't know if your attorney had any statement that they wanted to make, or can we begin the questioning?

chapters.summary: Ella Jung, partner at Sanford Heisler Sharp McKnight, says the firm represents whistleblowers against powerful corporations, argues local, state, and federal governments have abdicated responsibility, and says whistleblowers raising existential AI threats need protection.
chapters.title: Ella Jung introduces whistleblower practice and warns of AI risks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Good morning, and good morning to the members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: My name is Ella Jung.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: I'm a partner at Semper Heisler Sharp McKnight, a national civil rights and public interest litigation firm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We represent employees who have the courage to speak up against powerful corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Including whistleblowers who expose serious threats to public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify, along with my client, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Devin Kim, about one of the defining challenges of our time, ensuring that the race to develop artificial intelligence does not come at the expense of human safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Local, state,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: and federal governmental bodies have abdicated their responsibility to protect society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Whistleblowers who raise existential threats to humanity often pay the ultimate price for doing so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Those whistleblowers need protection, and you are in the body who can provide that protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: This body, the New York City Council, has an urgent obligation to protect the employees of New York City who raise issues designed to protect the public and who act in the public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: There's no more urgent matter facing the city council and indeed every city council, state government and federal body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We are already at a point of extreme vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Mass destruction, societal chaos, and extreme danger are all potentially minutes, days, or weeks away, as you have heard during the October 5th hearing.

chapters.summary: Jung says the firm represents Kim in his whistleblower retaliation lawsuit against XAI and SpaceX, that Kim raised safety and compliance concerns about Grok and was retaliated against, and lists clients including AI fraud, cyber sexual abuse victims, privacy breach victims, and algorithmic bias targets.
chapters.title: Jung describes Kim's retaliation suit and whistleblower client categories

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: AI has extraordinary potential to benefit humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: But its rapid development also presents extraordinary risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: And the people who often know the most about those risks are the engineers, researchers, and safety professionals working inside AI companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Unfortunately, like my client, speaking up can come at an enormous personal cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Our firm currently represents Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Kin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: his whistleblower retaliation lawsuit against XAI and SpaceX.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: As alleged in our complaint, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Kim raised serious concerns about AI safety and compliance related to Grok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Rather than having those concerns properly addressed, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Kim suffered retaliation and ultimately lost his job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Kim's case illustrates that we cannot rely on AI companies to self-regulate, and we should not allow them to harm individual employees who are willing to sacrifice their careers and livelihoods to protect the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: In my law firm,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We routinely represent whistleblowers like Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Kim, who stand opposed to illegal and or unethical behavior and individuals harmed by AI, including executives and employees at companies who are retaliated against for speaking out about corporate wrongdoing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: That corporate wrongdoing often involves AI fraud.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Digital ad fraud, and misrepresenting cybersecurity risks and control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Engineers, researchers, data scientists, and trust and safety staff at Frontier AI Labs who raise concerns about model safety, testing, deployment, and data practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: And who are often the first to be punished for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: They are often fired, demoted, sidelined, or pressured out after raising concerns for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: with their employers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Victims of cyber sexual abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: These victims have their intimate images posted on social media and manipulated by chatbots or are stalked, surveilled, spoofed, or deepfaked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Employees, customers, and users of technology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: who are victims of privacy and data breaches, which include unauthorized collection of biometric and employee data and unconsented use of personal information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: In addition to those areas, whistleblower protections should also extend to holding tech companies accountable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: for the harm created by their products, including AI tools, how it was designed, what safeguards were built into it, and whether those safeguards were implemented and activated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Whistleblower protections should also extend to incidences of algorithmic

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Employers use software to screen resumes, rank candidates, score video interviews, set pay, assign shifts, and decide who is promoted or let go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: When those tools produce outcomes that disadvantage people because of their age, race, sex,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: disability or another protected characteristic, the employer should be held liable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Meaningful whistleblower protections are essential.

chapters.summary: Jung says New York City can model responsible AI governance, points to SEC whistleblower incentives and California SB 53, and recommends three safeguards: anti-retaliation protections with remedies, secure reporting mechanisms, and financial rewards for whistleblowers.
chapters.title: Jung urges NYC to adopt SEC-style and California-style whistleblower protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: New York City has an

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: to help establish a model for responsible AI governance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We must ensure that the people who come forward are protected from retaliation, that their identities remain confidential,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: and that the law reach serious AI safety risks that may not fit neatly within existing regulatory violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We can learn from successful whistleblower programs at the federal level, including the SECs, which demonstrate how meaningful financial incentives can encourage individuals to expose wrongdoing that might otherwise remain hidden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: We can also learn from California, which has taken an important step through SB 53,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: signed into law last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: That bill established transparency requirements for frontier AI developers and protections for employees who report serious AI safety risks.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you conclude, please?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have some questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Therefore, I encourage the Council to establish three essential safeguards for AI whistleblowers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: One, strong anti-retaliation protections with meaningful remedies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Two, secure and effective reporting mechanism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: And three, financial rewards that recognize the extraordinary risks that whistleblowers undertake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: No whistleblower should ever have to sacrifice their future to protect ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Thank you for hearing me out, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ella Jung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin explains the Council's whistleblower bill would provide financial rewards from penalties and asks Kim whether SpaceX AI used NDAs or confidentiality policies that restricted reporting safety concerns; Kim says all employees signed NDAs and that restriction was strongly implied.
chapters.title: Menin asks Kim about whistleblower rewards and NDAs

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you both for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I do have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim, you mentioned that one of the things that you really want to see is strong whistleblower protection.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So our bill, for example, has a financial reward for whistleblowers and gives the whistleblower a significant

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: portion of the financial penalties which can result in the multi-millions of dollars since it is

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: a per agent per instance penalty so if there are thousands of rogue agents or the product is being sold and marketed in New York to

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: tens of thousands of people, obviously these penalties will add up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I appreciate your comments on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Also, the idea of the protection for the whistleblowers, this is exactly why at our hearing last week, when we had Alex Turner here, we issued a friendly subpoena

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: so that he could freely testify.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So to that end, when you were employed by Space XAI, was there any nondisclosure or confidentiality policies that could be interpreted as restricting employees from reporting safety concerns?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, but yes, all employees were required to sign an NDA on joining the company.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And were you ever instructed that if you were to speak out or raise certain safety concerns, that would be something that would violate the NDA?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Not explicitly, but I believe that was strongly implied in the way that the company was run.

chapters.summary: Menin asks Kim to describe the specific safety gaps that concerned him most and what safeguards he recommended before deployment; Kim says models should undergo refusal training to refuse dangerous queries like bioweapon development, and XAI released several models without those safeguards.
chapters.title: Menin asks Kim to describe safety gaps and recommended safeguards

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And you allege that you repeatedly warned SpaceX AI leadership that Grok could facilitate the creation of bioweapons and other dangerous activities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you describe the specific safety gaps that concerned you the most and what safeguards you might have recommended before deployment?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Yes, typically before companies release models, they undergo safety training, and they also undergo a specific type of safety training called refusal training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Models are trained or should be trained to refuse dangerous queries, such as assisting in the development of bioweapons or other weapons that would be very harmful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And this is also notably the kind of information that is very difficult to obtain today and other means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And at the time when XAI was releasing one of their earlier, or I should say, several models, we did not have those safeguards in place.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether Kim was able to issue safety warnings to more senior leadership before termination; Kim says he was, and that many employees and researchers were unhappy with how XAI handled the issue.
chapters.title: Menin asks if Kim's warnings reached senior leadership

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So you mentioned that you had discussed these safety concerns with your supervisor.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Were you ever able to issue these safety warnings higher up to more senior leadership before you were terminated?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I was, and this was also a very controversial issue with NXAI that many employees and researchers were very unhappy with.

chapters.summary: Menin asks what minimum testing and red-team procedures frontier AI developers should complete; Kim identifies missing critical thresholds for bioweapon and cyber capabilities, documentation justifying deployment, and testing for loss of control and manipulation capabilities as gaps in XAI releases.
chapters.title: Kim outlines minimum testing, evaluation, and red-team standards

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And based on your experience inside the company, what minimum testing, evaluation, and red team procedures should frontier AI developers be required to complete before releasing any model to the public?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: There are a number of very critical safety gaps that are present in XAI's model releases that are not present in other companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: One gap is critical thresholds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Companies typically commit to not releasing models above what they consider to be critical thresholds, whether that is in bioweapon capabilities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: cyber capabilities, and other dangerous capabilities that the model have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: A second...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: A second part of these releases that is very critical is a documentation justification for deployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Typically what that looks like is explaining what sort of critical thresholds were reached and what work was done to mitigate those thresholds and their justification for why they believe this model is safe before releasing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And then especially, and then a third critical piece that is becoming increasingly relevant is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Companies should be testing for loss of control and manipulation capabilities of these models before releasing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And specifically, these are standards that many companies have today, but are notably absent in the XCI safety releases.

chapters.summary: Menin notes Castillo-Madrid claimed not to know about Kim's termination and asks if that is accurate; Kim says it is surprising, and that during his time XAI had only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after he resigned.
chapters.title: Menin asks Kim about Castillo-Madrid's testimony and safety staffing

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Gabriela Castillo-Madrid, the Senior Manager of Global Government Affairs at SpaceX AI, who testified before you did.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I don't know if you had the opportunity to hear all of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But when I asked her about the circumstances around your termination, she said she was not aware.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Of any of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that a, and she was under oath, is that a factually accurate statement that she said?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If you know that is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: That would be difficult for me to know, but that is a surprising statement, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I don't know if you had the opportunity to hear the rest of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She kept saying that the company is dedicated to safety.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She kept saying that that was one of their top priorities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What did you think overall of her testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Well, as an early employee at XAI, I worked on the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And because of that, I had a very critical part in developing Grok and had held close relationships with many of the researchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And I was trusted with many important responsibilities within the company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And I use that standing to advocate for safety and other important things that I believe that the company should be doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And so I will note that if it was difficult for me to speak up and make changes that I believe were necessary within the company from my position, then I can only imagine for other people what that might be like for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I will also note that during my time at the company, I believe that this is an important problem to be working on, and therefore I spent significant time towards this effort in a personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: However, during my time there, there were only three employees working on

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I think in large part also due to the frustration with how safety was being handled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I can't speak to how AI safety is handled today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: It's been a year since I was an employee at the company, but if it's anything resembling what I personally experienced, then I would say that's a very troublesome state of affairs for them to be in.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how many employees XAI had overall when there were only three safety employees; Kim says technical staff involved in training and development numbered in the 200s, and says it is not credible that the senior global government affairs manager would not know safety staffing.
chapters.title: Menin asks about total technical staff versus safety staff

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So you're saying that a year ago there were three safety employees in the company working on safety around AI?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And in comparison to at that time a year ago, how many employees can you answer where they're at the company overall?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Well, it really depends how you're counting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: We had a large number of AI tutors who were responsible for training the model, and they were contractors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: We had a large number of data center employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I believe that in terms of technical staff that were involved in the direct training and development of the model, the number that I recall is in the 200s.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the idea that there were only three people dedicated to safety, and when I asked Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Castillo-Madrid how many employees were dedicated to safety, she told me she could not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that credible that the senior manager of global government affairs at SpaceX AI would not actually know how many safety employees would exist at the company?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I will say it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
