utterances.text: What is credible is if she is not deeply involved in understanding the day-to-day of the safety development of the company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I say this because I had strong relationships with the two formal legal counsels during my tenure at XAI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: The reason we had a strong relationship is because I would point out issues going on within the company or with the Brock model and would also propose and implement solutions to be solving those problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And we were able to develop a strong relationship that way and making their jobs easier and helping the company do the right thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I think given the level of detail that I heard today, I'm not...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I wouldn't feel comfortable that she would have the same level of detail and understanding.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether XAI uses outside third-party validators free of conflicts; Kim says not to his knowledge. Menin then describes finding a highly sexualized image of herself on regular Grok within 30 seconds and asks why SpaceX AI continues to allow it; Kim says he cannot speak to current standards but was told tasteful nudity was acceptable.
chapters.title: Menin asks Kim about third-party validation and Grok sexualized images

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Two more questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is the company currently, to your knowledge, validating the models with outside third-party validators who are free from conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And lastly, I don't know if you heard the earlier part of the questioning, but I pointed out that within 30 seconds this morning, I was able to ask Rock to do a sexualized image of myself, and there was a...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Uber sexualized image of myself under my official portrait.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I question Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Castillo-Madrid about why is this continued to be allowed by Grok?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This idea that within seconds,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These images and this was this was in just the regular grok free app not even the spicy mode This was just regular grok within less than 30 seconds an image

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That if my daughter saw would be horrified if other and this is just something that's readily available Why do you think that space XAI is continuing to allow this to happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to speak to the standards today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: However, the standards and directive that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: were shared with us when I was an employee was that a tasteful nudity is acceptable and is the goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I now will note that, you know, the tasteful is subjective and there was no clear person designated as to what the line should be there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The issue that I have with that is there was nothing tasteful about the image that we found.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And in fact, you could easily ask Rock to make it more sexualized.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so that was a prompt that Rock accepted.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we had successive images, each of which would become more sexualized, more offensive.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So this idea that it was like tasteful nudity or tasteful is just, you know, preposterous.

chapters.summary: Menin says the image was not tasteful and that Grok accepted prompts to make it more sexualized, thanks Kim for his courage and bravery, and passes questioning to Chair De La Rosa.
chapters.title: Menin thanks Kim and turns questioning to Chair De La Rosa

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kim, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I really want to thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I'm going to turn it over to my colleagues who I know have questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But I just want to thank you for your courage and bravery in coming forward and in speaking with us today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now I'm going to pass it over to Chair De La Rosa.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa thanks Kim and asks about a 2025 statement by an XAI co-founder that he would rather release an unsafe model than a poor-performing one; Kim says early on he was told XAI could not focus on safety while losing to competitors, but after Grok 3 launched, safety hiring was still blocked.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks Kim about XAI co-founder prioritizing unsafe models

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker, and I want to agree with her.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It takes a lot of courage and bravery for you and your attorney to be here as well and really give us some insight into your experience, which is horrific.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to ask you, in 2025, one of AXI's co-founders indicated that he would rather, quote, release an unsafe model than a poor performing one.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that that is still the priority for XAI in the development of their models?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I can't speak to the priority, but what I'm able to share is that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: especially in the early days of development, I was told that because the company was in a position where we were losing or had worse models than a lot of our competitors, it would be difficult for us to focus on safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And that once we were able to have a more competitive stance, then we would be able to focus more on safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And so at the time, that is a position that made sense to me and something that, you know, I really believed in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And so myself and many other employees, you know, I think a lot of people want to have see the work have positive impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I think many people want to believe that they are the good guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And if they are the ones developing powerful AI, that they would be doing a better job or a more moral job than the others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And so I think many people marched on with that belief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: However, in practice, I think what we saw, you know, after many, many months of sacrifice, I mean, personally, for me, I lived at the office for four months because I was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: working at all hours of the day, including weekends, because I was so dedicated to the mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Once we launched Grok 3, which at the time was actually the most intelligent model in the world, and so powerful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: powerful and so surprising to many of our competitors that OpenAI reportedly declared a code red and sort of trying to understand how XA had caught up so quickly and trying to do something about the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Even at that point, it was very difficult to advocate for safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Hiring for safety had count was being blocked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And so I think that is the point at which many people started having the realization, oh, maybe what was sort of told to us before isn't actually the case.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks whether other employees who spoke up were terminated and whether anything changed at Grok after Kim's departure; Kim says he cannot speak to those matters.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks if other employees were terminated and if Grok changed

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that other employees, to your knowledge, who were maybe afraid to speak up or were challenged in the same way that you were challenged when they did speak up, ended up being terminated as well?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And in terms of what you've witnessed now that you're on the other side of this, trying to create safety around AI,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: do you believe that anything has changed at Grok since your departure?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to speak to that.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa recalls Kim's testimony that management said safeguards are useless and AI will kill us all anyway, contrasts it with Castillo-Madrid's repeated safety claims, and asks whether safety is really at the heart of the company; Kim points to significant gaps in XAI's model cards and safety documentation.
chapters.title: De La Rosa contrasts 'AI will kill us anyway' with SpaceX safety testimony

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, one of the things that was, you know, very alarming from your testimony is that you said that when you raised this up to management, they said safeguards are useless and

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: AI will kill us all anyway.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You know, that is a very real statement to be made from a company who just testified under oath to this council that safety, I mean, I think that if we had a ringer every time she said safety,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: the bells would still be ringing here in the council.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Safety is the priority.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We do not deploy models without safety.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We ensure that there is safety.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: There is always a human being who's in charge of safety.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They said it in so many different ways.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But yeah, you're testifying today that your direct supervisors who understood the work you were doing said.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: AI would kill us anyway.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that safety is really at the heart of what this company is?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: is projecting.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks whether SpaceX's safety protocols align with regulations for space exploration and other areas; Kim says current laws and regulations around AI development are deeply inadequate.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks Kim about AI regulation and SpaceX safety protocols

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Well, I will again note that there is a significant gap in the model card or sort of safety documentation that in the releases that XAI puts out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: And I think the sort of explanation that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Well, we started later and we haven't had as much time doesn't really work anymore, given that meta who, you know, started later and the AI race and was able to build a team fairly quickly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: do have the higher safety standards that I mentioned earlier in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yeah, understanding legal constraints, and maybe you weren't working on this, but another part of her testimony this morning was about how, of course, we're safe.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're launching rockets.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that, you know, there are safety protocols?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are in line with regulations for the type of space exploration and other things that the company is exploring at this time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: I believe that the current set of laws and regulations around AI development are deeply inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for your questions.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa thanks Kim and his attorney for their bravery and insight, says the Council will use the testimony in its legislative process, then opens public testimony and explains decorum, two-minute speaking limits, and how to submit written testimony.
chapters.title: De La Rosa thanks Kim and opens public testimony

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Council members, we're good?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much for your questions and, again, for your bravery today and for being here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We really appreciate you giving us insight and understand that there is trauma associated with your departure from the company and the way you were treated.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so we really appreciate you giving us some insights and helping us to work around our legislative process to make sure that other workers are protected in this space.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony, and I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and the decorum should be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table, and furthermore, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's topic, which is the continuing discussion about the risk posed by artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If you have written statements,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings are not accepted.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa calls up Megan Lagerquist, Bryce Rogers, Gary O. Stephen, Kalima Amdakar, and Stephen Kramer, asking them to correct their names for the record.
chapters.title: De La Rosa calls first public panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I now call up the next panel, Megan Lagerquist, Bryce Rogers, Gary O.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Stephen, Kalima Amdakar, and I apologize, please correct your names for the record, and Stephen Kramer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Devin Kim

chapters.summary: Bryce Rogers of the Resisting Automated Disempowerment Collective says RAD wants AI tools to be safe and frontier advancement slowed, recommends strengthening Council Member Murano's chatbot privacy bill with affirmative consent for data collection, storage, use, and sale, and expanding it to agentic AI.
chapters.title: Bryce Rogers presents RAD Collective recommendations on chatbot privacy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: My name is Bryce Rogers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: I'm co-lead of the Resisting Automated Disempowerment Collective, or RAD Collective, a grassroots New York City community advocating for city and state policy that protects human life, joy, and democracy as AI and big tech grow more powerful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: We thank the council for reconvening today to finish the job that started last Monday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Rad wrote a letter to the council with feedback on all 10 introductions, but today my colleague Megan and I want to share more granular recommendations on two introductions in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Council member Murano's chatbot privacy bill and Speaker Menon's third party validation bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: But first, I'll straightforwardly share two strategic postures Rad assumes in sharing these recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: One, our goal is for AI tools served to New Yorkers to be safe and also to slow down the rate of advancement of frontier AI, given the recklessness and rapid power concentration we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Two, our angle with our recommendations today is for this legislation to pass and for companies to comply with it, as opposed to something like signaling or

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: intentionally extreme compliance burdens to trigger some sort of legal battle or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: I'll speak on affirmative consent in Murano's chatbot privacy introduction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Many users share deeply personal information with rich context when using AI products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Tropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and SpaceX AI, by default, collect user chat data and train their models on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Some of these companies, like Meta and OpenAI, use personal data for targeted advertising, and Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft combine this data with other information they've collected across their platforms to build a more complete profile of the user.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: This is invasive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Others, like Anthropic, insist they won't sell user data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: But as long as this is voluntary policy, they can walk it back anytime they need the revenue boost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: When Anthropic initially launched Claude, they did not train models on user data and automatically deleted it after 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: In September 2025, they rolled this back to an opt-out regime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: We recommend paring down Murano's bill to focus on the core requirements of affirmative consent for data collection, storage, use, and sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: It should also be expanded to cover data collected by agentic AI, not just chatbots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: This ensures the strongest version of the most impactful consumer protections can move forward into law as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to you hearing from my colleague, Megan.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, and please submit the testimony as well so we can review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: Sure thing.

chapters.summary: Megan Lagerquist of RAD Collective supports independent evaluations of high-risk frontier models, says companies currently control evaluator access and can release models regardless of findings, and calls for evaluators to have full model access and authority to block unsafe sales to New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Megan Lagerquist urges independent third-party audits with full access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Megan Lagerquist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: I am also a member of the RAD Collective, and I thank the Council for hearing my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: The second policy we want to address regards third-party audits, which Speaker Menon has proposed through Introduction 1100.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: RAD supports independent evaluations of high-risk frontier models defined by the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: Currently, many AI companies voluntarily work with AI third-party evaluators to run safety evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: However, the companies very much control access to what information they get and can decide to move forward with development or release regardless of the findings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: Meter employees who investigated the open AI hacked of Hugging Face reported that they were not provided with sufficient time to fully evaluate the incident and they only had logs from a constrained time window.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: To ensure that these products are safe for consumers, we must require independent verification that these models are sufficiently aligned with human instructions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: do not engage in social engineering or manipulation, and that the company's safeguards and monitoring and containment systems are equipped to control their own products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: We cannot rely on self-published model cards and even whistleblowers for full transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: Evaluators need to be guaranteed access to all documents and models they deem necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: They need to be able to run their own experiments, and that means more than just accessing chain of thought logs, although human-readable chain of thought

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: is important to preserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: They have to be able to see inside the model architecture to truly be effective at alignment auditing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: And if they say that the models do not meet New York's legal threshold for safety, these models should not be allowed to be sold to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: In order to effectively facilitate and enforce this regulation, the students need to invest in expanding the capacity of the Office of Technology and Innovation because, as we heard from Cyber Command's testimony on October 5th, they do not have the expertise to regulate industry as it stands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: There are independent AI safety research organizations that could fill the need for evaluators, but the council needs to build the legal support system to certify and empower them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: I will say the federal government is content with voluntary commitments and no verification, but I believe that this council is not content, and I urge you to move forward with strong public oversight of the AI industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Lagerquist
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Kalima with Demilitarized Brooklyn Navy Yard says public land is leased to tech companies like Radical AI that develop AI for hypersonic missiles and military surveillance, argues the tech industry cannot self-regulate, and asks the committee to examine whether Navy Yard tenants align with its public mission.
chapters.title: Kalima criticizes Brooklyn Navy Yard tech tenants and military AI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Thank you to the City Council for this opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: My name is Kalima and I'm here with Demilitarized Brooklyn Navy Yard, which is a grassroots campaign to get weapons manufacturers off of public land.

utterances.text: The DBNY campaign is here to hold the Brooklyn Navy Yard accountable for its role in using AI to further the U.S.

utterances.text: Military industrial complex.

utterances.text: Companies like Amazon, Google, and Apple make millions of dollars through contracts with the Department of War that are used to spy on communities abroad and at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: AI is not the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: It is another tool of the rich to exploit and surveil everyday people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: The Brooklyn Navy Yard uses public resources to lease to tech companies that use AI to develop weapons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: We have watched schools and homes be destroyed by American bombs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: We cannot turn away as our tax dollars and public land are used to destroy communities across the globe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: The tech industry is incapable of regulating itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: We see the cozy relationship between the tech industry and the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Military, as well as the increased use of AI and surveillance of racialized communities by entities like the NYPD and ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: DBNY wants these fascist tech companies off of our public land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: This is not what New Yorkers want or tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: dollars to be paying for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: The Brooklyn Navy Yard's role in housing tech companies that work with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Military makes them complicit in the war crimes that the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Is committing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: DBNY is asking this committee to do its job and to examine the tech companies leasing public land at the Brooklyn Navy Yard to ensure that they are actually in line

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: with the Navy Yard's mission to support the greater good, instead of contributing to ecocide, genocide, and deportations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Our public land should be used to provide community resources, services, and education, not to create new technologies that will infringe on our human rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kalima
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.text: Good afternoon or morning still.

utterances.text: Three years ago, I sent out an automated call that mimicked the voice of the president.

utterances.text: It was a warning shot to the entire industry as well as to America about what's coming, about what was in the future at the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: Little did I know that it wasn't the future I was predicting, it was the present at the time of things that were already going on in the mainstream all over the place, whether it be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: against individuals and sexualizing them, whether it be against politicians, including our mayor and other people here in Manhattan that were affected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask you all to think to the future now, because what we're seeing right now happened three years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: What we're seeing right now was preventable, is preventable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: But what we're seeing right now isn't AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: AI is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: Many years ahead of us right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: And the fact that it's being governed by

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: companies that aren't really governing it and by itself, meaning the artificial intelligence, means that the bad actors that I was accused of being aren't even human.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: And the safeguards that you put in here, not just today, but in the present,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: have to predict the future, and that's a very difficult job for anybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: I sympathize with both what's going on in the hearing today as well as the former hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: I hope that you think ahead when making your next steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Kramer
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: Committee on Technology held an oversight hearing continuing discussion of artificial intelligence risks, featuring testimony from SpaceX/XAI's Gabriela Castillo-Madrid and whistleblower Devin Kim.
Council members questioned SpaceX/XAI about safety staffing, third-party validation, sexualized deepfakes, medical data, liability, and whistleblower retaliation.
Public witnesses and attorney Ella Jung urged independent audits, whistleblower protections, and stronger AI oversight; the hearing ended with calls for continued legislation.
